about.title: Fillmore Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Fillmore's mix of small-town retail along A Street, older properties near Ventura Street, and agricultural or event venues means fall hazards look different from what you'd find in a big city. A wet floor at a local market, a broken step outside a downtown business, or poor lighting in an apartment parking area can all lead to serious injury. California law generally requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn visitors. That's why acting quickly matters: photographing the scene, getting witness names, and asking the business to preserve any surveillance footage before it's erased can make a real difference. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves, but we can connect you at no cost with an independent attorney who understands how these claims play out in Ventura County and can evaluate what happened to you.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Fillmore Fall

items.title: Notice Has to Be Proven
items.desc: Under California law, you generally must show the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to act. An attorney can help gather evidence, like maintenance logs or prior complaints, to support that.

items.title: Video Evidence Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Fillmore businesses overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help present your side clearly instead of letting an insurer's version stand unchallenged.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Fillmore?
items.answer: California generally gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, such as a city building or public sidewalk, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim. Because these timelines are unforgiving, it's worth speaking with an attorney sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I fell at a business on Ventura Street or A Street and no one wrote up a report?
items.answer: A missing incident report doesn't end your claim, but it does make documentation more important. Photos of the hazard, your shoes, and the surrounding area, plus names of anyone who saw the fall, can help fill that gap. An attorney can also send a formal request asking the business to preserve any video before it's deleted.

items.question: Will I have to prove the store or landlord actually knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, generally you need to show the owner either knew about the dangerous condition or should have known through reasonable inspection. This is often the most contested part of a premises liability case. An independent attorney can help investigate things like cleaning schedules, prior complaints, or how long the hazard existed.
